title: SR&ED Eligibility for Partnerships and Trusts | Canada FAQ
description: Under Canada's SR&ED program, partnerships and trusts can benefit but are not treated like CCPCs. See how eligibility works.
summary: Under Canada's federal SR&ED program, partnerships and trusts can benefit but are not treated like CCPCs. Certain trusts earn the basic 15% investment tax credit, with 40% of unclaimed credits refundable. Partnerships act as flow-through entities: SR&ED expenditures are deducted at the partnership level, while the resulting credit is allocated to partners, generally non-refundable and subject to at-risk rules.

Certain trusts earn the basic 15% investment tax credit, with 40% of unclaimed credits refundable. Partnerships act as flow-through entities: SR&ED expenditures are deducted at the partnership level, while the resulting credit is allocated to partners, generally non-refundable and subject to at-risk rules.
Executive Legislative and Fiscal Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the cornerstone of federal industrial and innovation policy in Canada. Administered jointly through a bifurcated governance model—wherein the Department of Finance Canada formulates statutory tax policy and drafts legislative amendments, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) executes technical and financial compliance reviews—the program delivers over $4.6 billion annually in federal tax relief across more than 24,000 corporate and unincorporated claimants. Small and medium-sized enterprises have historically accounted for approximately 64% of all claims filed, receiving roughly $1.5 billion in direct support during the 2024–2025 fiscal period, while software development has grown to represent 42.6% of all Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) allowed in 2025–2026, up from 35.7% in 2021–2022.

At its statutory core, the federal SR&ED regime operates through two distinct yet interdependent provisions of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the "Act"). First, subsection 37(1) of the Act establishes a dedicated expenditure pooling mechanism that permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current—and, following recent legislative restoration, capital—SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada directly against current-year business income, or to carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and section 127.1 of the Act authorize the generation of a federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on "qualified expenditures," which may be applied to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable or, for eligible corporations and individuals, received as a direct cash refund via cheque or direct deposit.

Between late 2024 and early 2026, the federal SR&ED architecture underwent its most significant statutory expansion in more than a decade. Following multi-phase industry consultations initiated in Budget 2024 (tabled April 16, 2024, which initially provisioned $600 million for future SR&ED enhancements alongside a $2.4 billion sovereign artificial intelligence compute strategy), the Department of Finance outlined initial reform parameters in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 2024) and released comprehensive draft legislative proposals on August 22, 2025. On November 4, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, under the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney, tabled Federal Budget 2025 (Canada Strong), which consolidated and further expanded these measures. The implementing legislation, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, bringing the statutory amendments into legal force retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, and for capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

The legislative enactment of Bill C-15 fundamentally alters the capital formation calculus for Canadian research enterprises through five structural reforms. First, with respect to the doubling of the enhanced expenditure limit, while the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the annual expenditure ceiling for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 increased the maximum annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, effectively doubling the maximum annual refundable enhanced credit from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, regarding the creation of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category, access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC was historically restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), a rule that penalized domestic technology and biotechnology firms that listed on public equity exchanges. Bill C-15 introduced the "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) definition under subsection 127(9) of the Act, granting qualifying Canadian-resident public corporations access to the identical 35% enhanced ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures.

Third, the legislation enacted an expansion and redesign of phase-out thresholds. For CCPCs, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out corridor—over which the enhanced expenditure limit is reduced to nil—was widened from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to a $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range. Furthermore, CCPCs may now formally elect under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to calculate their expenditure limit reduction using the three-year average gross revenue test ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000) that is mandatory for ECPCs, thereby preventing capital-intensive but pre-revenue or low-revenue private enterprises from losing access to the 35% rate simply due to high balance-sheet equity or debt. Fourth, reversing the 11-year exclusion enacted in 2014, Bill C-15 reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b) and amended section 127 of the Act to restore both immediate 100% income deductibility and ITC eligibility (with 40% refundability for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs) for depreciable capital property and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Fifth, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA instituted an optional upfront administrative pre-claim approval regime via My Business Account, providing eligible corporations and partnerships with binding technical project determinations within eight weeks prior to or shortly after commencing R&D activities.

These SR&ED reforms operate alongside the broader Productivity Super-Deduction introduced in Budget 2025, which lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment to 13.2%. The Productivity Super-Deduction reinstates the Accelerated Investment Incentive, provides 100% immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing capital assets across Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software), and introduces a temporary 100% immediate deduction for eligible manufacturing and processing (M&P) buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025 and used before 2030 (where at least 90% of floor space is used for manufacturing or processing goods for sale or lease), with the deduction rate phasing down to 75% in 2030–2031 and 55% in 2032–2033. While Class 1 M&P buildings remain excluded from SR&ED capital expenditure claims, the concurrent availability of temporary 100% M&P building expensing and restored SR&ED equipment credits allows industrial innovators to shelter both facility envelopes and internal laboratory apparatus simultaneously.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Eligibility Jurisprudence
The Subsection 248(1) Statutory Framework and Excluded Activities

Eligibility for federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives is anchored strictly in the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statute defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three primary categories of scientific or technological endeavour, supplemented by a fourth category of restricted support work. The first category, basic research under paragraph (a), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Because basic research lacks immediate commercial utility, it is predominantly performed within university laboratories and specialized research institutes rather than by commercial corporate claimants. The second category, applied research under paragraph (b), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third category, experimental development under paragraph (c), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the overwhelming majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada.

The fourth category, support work under paragraph (d), encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. A critical legal distinction governs paragraph (d) support activities: computer programming, engineering design, or mathematical analysis are never eligible for SR&ED in isolation. They qualify only to the extent that their scope and scale are strictly proportional ("commensurate with the needs") and causally necessary ("directly in support") to resolve the underlying scientific or technological uncertainty of a core basic research, applied research, or experimental development project conducted in Canada.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) of the Act codifies explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k) that disqualify commercial, aesthetic, and routine operational activities even where they occur alongside genuine innovation. These expressly excluded activities encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes (including cosmetic, ergonomic, or aesthetic modifications lacking underlying technological uncertainty); and routine data collection (unless directly in support of, and commensurate with, an active SR&ED experimentation loop under paragraph (d)). Furthermore, the CRA's administrative guidance underscores that commercial novelty, functional uniqueness, or the acquisition of existing industry know-how does not establish a technological advancement. A product may be entirely new to a company's commercial catalogue or the domestic marketplace without the underlying development work constituting SR&ED if the engineering relied upon standard methodologies known to competent professionals in the field.
The Five-Question Legal Test Versus the CRA Two-Step Administrative Methodology

The judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) is governed by the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998), authored by Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman. In Northwest Hydraulic, the Court synthesized the statutory definition into five cumulative criteria—universally referred to in Canadian tax jurisprudence as the Five Questions—which every claimant bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities. First, the Court asks whether there was a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedure; if the resolution of a problem is attainable through standard practice or predictable adjustments by a competent professional in the relevant field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, the inquiry examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that scientific or technological uncertainty. Third, the Court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. As earlier established by the Tax Court of Canada in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363), a "systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and of highly accurate measurements and analyses," thereby excluding unguided trial-and-error tinkering or intuitive troubleshooting. Fourth, the test asks whether the process resulted in a scientific or technological advancement. Crucially, a project does not need to succeed commercially or even achieve its targeted technical performance to generate a technological advancement; the definitive rejection of a scientifically plausible hypothesis through rigorous experimentation advances the stock of technological knowledge by proving why a given technical approach fails under specific constraints. Fifth, the Court requires proof that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.

In August 2021, the CRA reorganized its administrative Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, condensing the five questions into a two-requirement framework—commonly termed the "Why and How" approach. Under the CRA's administrative manual, Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) evaluate, first, why the work was conducted (whether it was undertaken to achieve a scientific or technological advancement by overcoming a scientific or technological uncertainty arising from an insufficiency in available knowledge), and second, how the work was conducted (whether it followed a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis). While the CRA designed the two-requirement framework to align administrative reviews with the text of subsection 248(1), recent Tax Court of Canada rulings confirm that the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test remains the binding legal standard in litigation. Consequently, an audit defence strategy that satisfies only a high-level narrative of "why and how" without explicitly evidencing hypothesis formulation, iterative experimental testing, and dated contemporaneous records will fail under judicial scrutiny.
Contemporary Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence (2024–2026)

Recent decisions from the Tax Court of Canada illustrate the decisive role of contextual uncertainty, quantitative metrics, and contemporaneous documentation across both traditional manufacturing and advanced technology sectors. In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, the appellant claimed SR&ED tax credits for experimental development undertaken to control microbial growth and achieve room-temperature shelf stability for a vinegar-based beverage. The Minister of National Revenue denied the claim on the grounds that the appellant utilized chemical preservatives—specifically potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and ultimately a natural mushroom-derived preservative, Chiber—that were already publicly known to competent food scientists, and alleged that the claimant failed to conduct a systematic investigation or maintain adequate technical records. Justice Bodie of the Tax Court of Canada overturned the Minister's reassessment and allowed the claim in full, establishing three vital legal propositions for SR&ED auditors and claimants. First, contextual technological uncertainty can exist even when a chemical compound, software algorithm, or engineering component is publicly available, provided that the known solution has never been applied or validated within the specific operational, chemical, or architectural constraints faced by the taxpayer. Second, contemporaneous documentation is legally sufficient when it tracks the hypotheses formulated, the experiments executed to test those hypotheses, and the empirical results obtained as the work progressed; it does not need to be formatted as a peer-reviewed academic treatise designed for an outsider unfamiliar with the industry to replicate. Third, despite the CRA's internal transition to the "how and why" assessment rubric, the five questions of Northwest Hydraulic remain the authoritative legal benchmark in the Tax Court of Canada.

By contrast, the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Biscuiterie Dominic inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 97) demonstrates the fatal consequences of conflating commercial product development with systematic experimental development. In Biscuiterie Dominic, two commercial bakery corporations claimed SR&ED across six food-processing projects involving natural preservatives for croissants, quinoa cookie formulations, and extending the shelf life of chocolate-filled pastries and filled croissants. The Court dismissed all six claims, highlighting four fatal evidentiary defects: first, the underlying ingredients and baking processes were standard industry knowledge, meaning no technological uncertainty existed that routine procedure could not resolve; second, the companies relied heavily on formulation recommendations provided directly by their ingredient suppliers rather than generating independent scientific hypotheses; third, the testing protocols were predominantly qualitative and subjective (relying on sensory evaluations of taste, appearance, and texture) rather than rigorous quantitative scientific measurements (such as water activity, pH levels, microbial colony counts, or rheological texture metrics); and fourth, scaling and integrating the recipes onto the commercial production line constituted routine industrial engineering.

Similarly, recent Tax Court decisions in DAZZM and Vortex Energy reinforce the evidentiary rule that oral witness testimony at trial cannot cure a lack of contemporaneous written records. In these cases, the Court acknowledged that the taxpayers' engineering teams tackled genuinely difficult technical challenges, yet denied the SR&ED claims under the fifth question of Northwest Hydraulic because the claimants could produce only static final design documents or post-facto reconstructions rather than versioned code repositories, dated failure logs, and iterative test metrics created during the taxation year.

Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363, TCC)

Rejected claims where claimants relied on supplier advice, used known methods, performed qualitative sensory tasting rather than quantitative scientific analysis (pH, water activity, microbial counts), and conducted routine line integration.
Held that credible oral testimony and technically complex work cannot overcome the absence of contemporaneous, dated records showing iterative hypothesis testing and intermediate failures.

body.text: Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Corporate Classifications, and Phase-Out Mechanics
Entity Classification and the Introduction of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

The quantum, rate, and cash refundability of federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits under section 127 and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act depend strictly upon the legal classification of the claimant throughout the taxation year. For decades, the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was restricted to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)—defined under subsection 125(7) of the Act as private corporations resident in Canada that are not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by any combination thereof. Under the legacy rules, if a CCPC completed an initial public offering (IPO) or reverse takeover on a stock exchange, it immediately forfeited eligibility for the 35% refundable credit and dropped to the 15% non-refundable basic rate.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 eliminated this structural disincentive by creating the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) under subsection 127(9) of the Act. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory conditions: first, it must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year; second, it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or internationally, or have validly elected (or been designated by the Minister) to be a public corporation under the Act; and third, it must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)) by one or more non-resident persons. Crucially, Canadian-resident subsidiaries at least 90% of whose issued shares of each class are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more ECPCs (eligible subsidiaries) also gain access to the enhanced 35% regime, provided the expenditure limit is shared across the consolidated corporate group. Foreign-controlled corporations (such as Canadian subsidiaries of United States, European, or Asian parent companies), public corporations controlled by non-residents, and large domestic corporations exceeding the $75,000,000 phase-out ceiling remain restricted to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC rate.

Unincorporated businesses—specifically sole proprietorships (individuals) and certain trusts—earn the basic 15% ITC rate, of which 40% of the unclaimed credit balance is refundable in cash. Partnerships, by contrast, are treated as flow-through conduits rather than autonomous taxpayers for ITC calculation purposes. Because a partnership cannot directly claim an ITC on a T2 or T1 return, SR&ED expenditures are deducted at the partnership level in computing net partnership income, while the resulting ITC is allocated to the respective partners at the end of the partnership's fiscal period via Form T661 and information slips. Because credits allocated to partners are generally non-refundable and subject to at-risk rules, tax governance best practice dictates incorporating an R&D venture as a CCPC prior to incurring substantial research expenditures.
Mathematical Mechanics of the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

Under subsection 127(10.1) of the Act, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC earns an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic ITC—yielding a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual Expenditure Limit defined in subsection 127(10.2). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline maximum Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Qualified expenditures incurred in excess of the corporation's Expenditure Limit earn the 15% basic ITC rate. To target fiscal support toward small and mid-sized domestic innovators, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is subject to a linear reduction ("grind") once the corporate group's capital or revenue scale exceeds statutory thresholds.
1. CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Post-December 15, 2024)

Unless a CCPC files a formal election to use the revenue-based method, its $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 of the Act, reported on federal Schedule 33, Line 690, and interpreted in archived CRA Bulletin IT-532) of the corporation for its immediately preceding taxation year, combined with the taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the phase-out begins when prior-year aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada (TC) exceeds $15,000,000 and reduces the Expenditure Limit linearly to $0 when TC reaches $75,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 corridor of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000):

Under the legacy rules for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the numerator and denominator constant was $40,000,000, reflecting the $50,000,000 − $10,000,000 span, multiplied against a $3,000,000 base limit.
2. Qualifying Corporation and Qualifying Income Limit Formula

To determine whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)—which governs whether the corporation receives 100% cash refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC (and 40% cash refundability on its 15% basic ITC on current expenditures above the expenditure limit)—the Act compares the corporation's prior-year taxable income to its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit is calculated as:

In this statutory equation, A is nil if the aggregate prior-year taxable capital amount (TC) is less than or equal to $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which TC exceeds $15,000,000. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula utilized $40,000,000 in place of $60,000,000 and a $10,000,000 threshold for A11.
3. ECPC and Elective CCPC Gross Revenue Phase-Out Method

Because public corporations frequently carry substantial share capital on their balance sheets following public equity issuances, applying a taxable capital test to ECPCs would prematurely disqualify public biotechnology and hardware companies that have little or no commercial revenue. Consequently, for an ECPC, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is phased out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based exclusively on the average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reflected in the corporation's financial statements (or the consolidated financial statements of the consolidated group, if the ECPC is a member of a group that prepares consolidated financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles).

In a highly consequential planning reform, Bill C-15 enacted subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), allowing a CCPC that is not associated with another corporation (subsection 127(10.31)), or a group of associated CCPCs acting jointly (subsection 127(10.32)), to elect in prescribed form to compute its Expenditure Limit reduction using this identical three-year average gross revenue test ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000) instead of taxable capital employed in Canada. For venture-backed Canadian startups and clean-technology developers that raise $20,000,000 to $75,000,000 in preferred equity or convertible debt (which inflates Part I.3 taxable capital) while remaining pre-revenue or generating under $15,000,000 in sales, filing the subsection 127(10.31) revenue election preserves the full $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds.
4. Short Taxation Years and Associated / Consolidated Group Allocations

If a corporation has a taxation year of fewer than 365 days (a short taxation year, frequently triggered by an acquisition of control under subsection 249(4) or corporate amalgamation), its Expenditure Limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (or 366 in a leap year). Furthermore, associated CCPCs (and ECPCs within a consolidated group) must allocate the single $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit among group members. However, subsection 127(10.22) provides a targeted deemed non-association relieving provision for expenditure limit purposes where a CCPC would be associated with another corporation solely because of paragraph 256(1.2)(a) (for example, because the same group of venture capital or angel investors holds shares in both corporations) and the two corporations do not have identical shareholders, provided the Minister is satisfied under subsection 127(10.23) that the corporations are not otherwise associated and that the difference in shareholdings was not created to meet this requirement.
Refundability, Carryforwards, and Income Inclusion Mechanics

The cash flow realization of SR&ED credits is governed by the refundability matrix of section 127.1 of the Act. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs operating within the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit, unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate are 100% refundable in cash for qualified current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), and 40% refundable in cash for qualified capital expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024. For qualifying CCPCs incurring expenditures above the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit, unclaimed ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate on current expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit are 40% refundable in cash provided the CCPC meets the "qualifying corporation" definition. Conversely, for ECPCs incurring expenditures above the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit, as well as for non-qualifying or foreign-controlled corporations across their entire expenditure pool, ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate are 0% refundable (strictly non-refundable). Individuals and unincorporated trusts earn the 15% basic rate, of which 40% is refundable on current and eligible capital expenditures.

Any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is not refunded in cash and is not utilized to offset Part I federal income tax payable in the current year may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5). Finally, federal SR&ED ITCs are subject to subsequent-year taxability. Whenever a federal ITC is claimed in Year T—whether applied to reduce Part I tax payable, carried back to a prior year, or received as a cash refund—the exact dollar amount of the federal ITC reduces the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year T + 1. If the taxpayer has already deducted its entire subsection 37(1) pool in Year T (resulting in a negative pool balance in Year T + 1 once the prior year's ITC is subtracted), that negative balance is brought directly into the taxpayer's taxable income in Year T + 1 pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Act.

body.text: Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Personnel Versus Specified Employees

Salaries and wages consistently constitute the largest expenditure component of Canadian SR&ED claims. Under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, only the portion of salaries and wages paid to employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (plus the employer's share of statutory payroll contributions such as Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Québec Pension Plan [QPP], and Employment Insurance [EI]) qualifies as an SR&ED expenditure. The CRA's administrative policy defines "directly engaged" strictly on the basis of hands-on technical tasks performed rather than an employee's corporate title or academic credentials. First-line technical supervisors who direct the experimental methodology of engineers, developers, or laboratory technicians qualify to the extent their supervision directly guides technical experimentation; conversely, C-suite executives or administrative managers whose involvement is limited to project budgeting, commercial roadmapping, or human resources management are excluded unless they personally perform hands-on experimental work or direct technical supervision. Furthermore, under subsection 78(4) of the Act, any salary or wage accrued at the end of a taxation year must be actually paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year to be deductible and eligible for SR&ED in that year.

Strict statutory anti-avoidance limitations apply to Specified Employees—defined in subsection 248(1) of the Act as any employee who either is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the claimant corporation or any corporation related to it, or does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder). For Specified Employees, four mandatory statutory restrictions govern claim calculations. First, any remuneration based on profits or any bonus paid to a Specified Employee is 100% excluded from SR&ED expenditures; consequently, founder-engineers must draw regular base salary (reported on T4 slips) rather than performance bonuses or dividends, as dividends represent distributions of after-tax corporate surplus and never qualify for SR&ED. Second, the maximum total direct SR&ED salary claimable for a Specified Employee in a taxation year is capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the employee was employed in the taxation year. Third, when calculating notional overhead under the Proxy Method (Part 5 of Form T661), the amount of a Specified Employee's salary that can flow into the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base is capped at the lesser of 75% of the Specified Employee's total salary and wages (before multiplying by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for short taxation years or partial-year employment. Fourth, where a Specified Employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations in the same year, the maximum salary cap must be shared among the associated group using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)). Across active audit periods, the statutory YMPE set by the CRA was $68,500 for 2024 (yielding a 2.5× YMPE proxy cap of $171,250 and a 5× YMPE direct cap of $342,500), $71,300 for 2025 (yielding a 2.5× YMPE proxy cap of $178,250 and a 5× YMPE direct cap of $356,500), and $74,600 for 2026 (yielding a 2.5× YMPE proxy cap of $186,500 and a 5× YMPE direct cap of $373,000).
Overhead and Other Expenditures: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus Traditional Method

In Part 3 of Form T661, a claimant must elect annually whether to account for SR&ED overhead and other indirect costs using the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or the Traditional Method. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the election between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is irrevocable for that taxation year. Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method—governed by subsection 127(9) of the Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations—the claimant does not track or itemize actual overhead expenses on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (incorporating the Specified Employee cap of min(75% × Total Salary, 2.5 × YMPE)). A critical accounting nuance applies to the PPA: because the corporation's actual overhead expenses (such as office rent, utilities, human resources, and administrative support salaries) are already deducted under section 9 of the Act in computing ordinary business income, the PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool. Instead, the PPA is added solely to "qualified expenditures" on Form T661 Part 4 and Part 5 for the purpose of generating the 35% or 15% federal ITC (and applicable provincial credits in jurisdictions that recognize the PPA, such as Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta).

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead itemizes and claims actual overhead and other expenditures in both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. To qualify under the Traditional Method, an overhead cost must be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (as defined under Income Tax Regulations paragraph 2902(a)), meaning the incremental cost would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out, alongside directly related clerical, administrative, and maintenance support salaries. From a second-order tax optimization perspective, the Proxy Method is superior for labour-intensive R&D enterprises (such as software engineering, artificial intelligence, and mathematical modelling firms), where a 55% notional uplift on developer salaries vastly exceeds incremental shop-floor overhead. Conversely, the Traditional Method can yield a higher net recovery for capital- and energy-intensive industrial manufacturing, metallurgy, or chemical processing operations where massive utility consumption, dedicated facility maintenance, and non-salaried shop-floor consumables exceed 55% of direct technical payroll.
Materials Consumed Versus Materials Transformed

Expenditures for materials qualify for SR&ED under both the Proxy and Traditional methods only if the materials are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass items that are destroyed, evaporated, or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of experimental testing, such as chemical reagents, biological culture media, destructive metallurgical test blanks, or fuel consumed during prototype engine dynamometer trials. Materials transformed encompass physical inputs that are integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig constructed to test a scientific or technological hypothesis, where the resulting item has no commercial value or is subsequently scrapped. If an experimental prototype or pilot plant incorporating transformed materials is later sold commercially or converted into a commercial production asset, the CRA enforces SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 37(1)(c.2) and 127(27)–(35) of the Act, clawing back the lesser of the fair market value or proceeds of disposition of the prototype and the historical material costs claimed for SR&ED.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and the 80% Inclusion Rule

When a claimant engages an external contractor in Canada to perform SR&ED work on its behalf, the tax treatment bifurcates based on whether the parties deal at arm's length. For arm's-length SR&ED contracts, the contract must be for the performance of basic research, applied research, experimental development, or commensurate paragraph (d) support work carried out in Canada on behalf of the claimant. While 100% of the eligible arm's-length contract payment is deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, subsection 127(9) restricts the inclusion for federal ITC purposes to 80% of the contract payment, applying a statutory 20% haircut to remove the subcontractor's presumed commercial profit margin from the federal tax credit base. Conversely, payments made to non-arm's-length subcontractors (such as a sister corporation or subsidiary) do not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer; instead, the performing entity must claim its own underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures or formally transfer those qualified expenditures to the payer. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit research consortia in Canada for SR&ED related to the claimant's business—where the claimant is legally entitled to exploit the results of the research—are subject to the 80% inclusion rule for federal ITC calculation. Crucially, payments to foreign subcontractors for R&D work performed outside Canada are 0% eligible for federal SR&ED, save for narrow, restricted allowances under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) for salaries of Canadian-resident employees temporarily performing indispensable testing outside Canada, capped at 10% of total Canadian directly engaged SR&ED salaries.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and capital lease costs were completely excluded from the SR&ED program. Enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), subsection 37(1)(b) and the capital expenditure provisions of section 127 were restored for property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). A nuanced statutory timing distinction exists in Bill C-15 that tax auditors must verify carefully: while the increase in the Expenditure Limit to $6,000,000 and the creation of ECPCs apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024, the in-force provision for restored capital expenditures under subsection 37(10) and the time-of-acquisition rule under subsection 127(11.2) apply to property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (when the property becomes "available for use"), even if the claimant's taxation year began prior to December 16, 2024. Where a claimant's taxation year straddles December 15, 2024, SR&ED operating time percentages for capital and leased equipment must be calculated specifically for the post-December 15, 2024 operating period.

Under the restored capital expenditure policy, four distinct sets of rules govern property and lease eligibility. First, for All or Substantially All (ASA) depreciable property (≥ 90% use), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property (such as specialized laboratory instruments, environmental testing chambers, on-premise AI GPU server clusters, 3D printers, or custom test rigs) qualifies in full (100% of capital cost, including purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, and freight) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either that the property would be used all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or that all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. Second, regarding new versus used capital property, both new and used depreciable property meeting the ≥ 90% ASA test qualify for immediate 100% income deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b). However, to earn the section 127 Investment Tax Credit (35% or 15%), the property must be new—meaning it was never used for any purpose whatever by any person or partnership prior to its acquisition by the claimant—as used equipment is strictly ineligible for the federal ITC. Furthermore, land (a non-depreciable asset) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings remain statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital claims.

Third, with respect to Shared-Use Equipment (SUE, > 50% to < 90% use), under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(11.5), if a claimant acquires new depreciable property after December 15, 2024 (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture [GPOEF]) that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold but is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE). SUE does not enter the subsection 37(1) deduction pool (it is depreciated via standard CCA schedules), but it earns an SR&ED ITC on 25% of its capital cost at the end of the "first term" (minimum 12 months after becoming available for use) and an additional 25% of its capital cost at the end of the "second term" (minimum 24 months after becoming available for use), for a total of 50% of capital cost qualifying for ITCs across two periods. Fourth, regarding lease costs of equipment incurred after December 15, 2024, equipment leased and used ASA (≥ 90% of operating time) is reported on Line 350 of Form T661, where 100% of post-December 15, 2024 lease costs qualify under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, except that claimants electing the Proxy Method must exclude lease costs for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF). Conversely, equipment leased and used primarily (50% to < 90% of operating time) is reported on Line 355 of Form T661; under the Proxy Method, the claimant may include 50% (half) of the post-December 15, 2024 lease costs (excluding GPOEF), whereas under the Traditional Method, no statutory provision permits partial lease claims between 50% and 89%, requiring the claimant to enter "0" on Line 355.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking
Statutory Interaction: Provincial Credits as "Government Assistance"

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which delivers R&D support through direct discretionary grants rather than the corporate tax return) and the Yukon territory administer statutory R&D tax credits that stack atop the federal SR&ED program. However, the combined financial recovery is never a simple arithmetic sum of the federal and provincial headline percentages. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, any provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED expenditures constitutes "government assistance". Consequently, provincial R&D credits must be deducted on Line 429 and Line 513 of federal Form T661, reducing both the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base in the same taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures are incurred.

One critical statutory exception mitigates this "assistance grind" for claimants electing the Proxy Method: under CRA policy and subsection 127(18), the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as Ontario's OITC or ORDTC) that is directly attributable to the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool, because the PPA is a notional proxy amount rather than an outlay or expenditure incurred by the taxpayer. Furthermore, if a corporation is unable to utilize a non-refundable provincial R&D tax credit (such as the Ontario ORDTC or the non-refundable half of the Manitoba credit) because it is in a tax-loss position and prefers to preserve its 35% refundable federal ITC base unreduced, several provinces permit the taxpayer to formally renounce the provincial tax credit (in Manitoba, for example, federal rules require the renunciation to be executed on or before six months after the corporation's taxation year-end, even though Manitoba's provincial statute allows up to one year after the filing due date).
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Stacking Mechanics

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario and conducting eligible SR&ED within the province can layer up to three distinct provincial tax credits administered by the CRA alongside their T2 Corporate Income Tax Return. First, governed by the Ontario Taxation Act, 2007 and claimed on T2 Schedule 566 (flowing to Schedule 5, Line 468), the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (100% of current expenditures, 100% of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, and 80% of eligible arm's-length contracts) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding a maximum annual cash credit of $240,000. Crucially, while Bill C-15 doubled the federal expenditure limit to $6,000,000, Ontario retained the $3,000,000 cap for the OITC, meaning Ontario expenditures between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000 earn the 35% federal ITC but $0 in OITC. Furthermore, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out linearly if the associated corporate group's prior-year Ontario taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if its prior-year Canadian taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000; where both tests are triggered, the phase-out ratios are multiplied together rather than taking the lesser. Notably, unlike the federal enhanced credit, the OITC does not require the claimant to be a CCPC, so a foreign-owned subsidiary operating an Ontario R&D centre within the income and capital thresholds can claim the 8% refundable OITC.

Second, claimed on T2 Schedule 508 (Schedule 5, Line 416), the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment regardless of size (with no statutory expenditure cap, though frequently modelled up to $500,000 in mid-market benchmarks). Unused ORDTC balances may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax payable. In the statutory ordering of calculations, the OITC constitutes government assistance that reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC, whereas the ORDTC does not reduce the OITC base. Both the OITC and ORDTC restored 100% eligibility for capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, as confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement. Third, claimed on T2 Schedules 568 and 569 (Schedule 5, Line 470), the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible research contract with an approved Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, hospital research institute, or non-profit research institute, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (representing a maximum annual credit of $4,000,000).
Exact Mathematical Stacking Demonstration (Ontario CCPC, $1,000,000 Eligible Current Spend)

To illustrate the exact statutory ordering, consider an Ontario CCPC with prior-year taxable income of $300,000 (<$500,000) and prior-year taxable capital of $5,000,000 (<$15,000,000) that incurs $1,000,000 of eligible current SR&ED expenditures in Ontario (assuming Traditional Method or non-PPA expenditures so that 100% of provincial assistance grinds the federal pool).

body.text: As this calculation demonstrates, if a loss-position Ontario startup cannot utilize the $32,200 non-refundable ORDTC for many years, claiming the ORDTC immediately reduces its federal qualified expenditure base by $32,200, costing the startup $32,200 × 35% = $11,270 in immediate cash refund from the federal ITC. Evaluating whether to waive or renounce non-refundable provincial credits is therefore an essential step in cash-constrained startup tax planning.
Québec: The March 25, 2025 Abolition of Legacy Credits and Launch of the Consolidated CRIC

Unlike Ontario, British Columbia, and Manitoba, the province of Québec administers an autonomous corporate income tax system through Revenu Québec (via the CO-17 Déclaration de revenus des sociétés return) under the Taxation Act (Québec). In its March 25, 2025 provincial budget (further detailed in Revenu Québec Tax News of July 9, 2025), the Government of Québec enacted a sweeping structural overhaul of its R&D tax incentive architecture. For taxation years of corporations (or fiscal periods of qualified partnerships) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec formally eliminated six legacy tax credits: first, the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.7); second, the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.6); third, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; fourth, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; fifth, the tax credit for technological adaptation services; and sixth, the industrial design component of the design tax credits.

In place of this fragmented legacy system (which previously offered rates between 14% and 30% depending on whether corporate assets fell below $50,000,000 to $75,000,000), Québec introduced a single consolidated powerhouse incentive: the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC). The CRIC transforms Québec R&D tax planning across four primary dimensions. First, it establishes a universal two-tier refundable rate structure with no asset cap: regardless of corporate asset size, ownership structure, or public or private status, any qualified corporation (or corporate member of a qualified partnership) maintaining an establishment and carrying on business in Québec earns a 100% refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures in excess of $1,000,000, with no upper ceiling on total claimable expenditures. Second, whereas federal SR&ED strictly terminates once technological uncertainty is resolved, the Québec CRIC extends tax credit eligibility downstream to pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec—including product certification, regulatory compliance trials, industrial design, and commercial-scale pilot validation necessary to bring an R&D innovation to market. Third, the CRIC explicitly encompasses capital expenditures incurred for the acquisition of depreciable property used in Québec R&D and pre-commercialization activities, alongside salaries and wages, subcontractor consideration, and payments to eligible research organizations. Fourth, to focus fiscal assistance on higher-value-added technical positions, a claimant's eligible expenditures for a taxation year must first be reduced by a modified exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold, calculated by multiplying the Québec basic personal income tax amount for the calendar year (such as $18,571 in 2025) by the proportion of time each employee devoted to eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. For example, a Québec enterprise employing 10 full-time R&D engineers in 2025 faces an exclusion threshold of 10 × $18,571 = $185,710 (since $185,710 > $50,000); only eligible expenditures above $185,710 earn the 30% and 20% CRIC rates.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Incremental Baseline Mechanics

Alberta collects and administers its own corporate income tax through Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) via the AT1 Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return. Governed by Division 7 of Part 6 (Sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Alberta (matching federal SR&ED eligibility rules).

The IEG employs a unique two-tier incremental rate architecture designed to reward year-over-year R&D expansion. First, a corporation's "base spending level" (reported on Line 118 of Form AT29 for non-associated corporations) is determined as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years (Line 114 plus Line 116 divided by 2). Second, under the Tier 1 base calculation (Part I on Form AT29), the corporation earns an 8% refundable credit on all current-year eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures up to the lesser of its current-year eligible spending and the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit. Third, under the Tier 2 incremental enhancement (Part II calculation on Form AT29), on the slice of current-year eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (capped at $4,000,000) that exceeds the corporation's two-year average Base Amount, the corporation earns an additional 12% refundable credit, bringing the total credit rate on incremental R&D growth to 20% (8% + 12%).

For example, if an Alberta corporation incurred $1,200,000 of eligible Alberta SR&ED in Year T − 2 and $1,800,000 in Year T − 1, its rolling Base Amount for Year T is ($1,200,000 + $1,800,000) / 2 = $1,500,000. If the corporation spends $3,000,000 on eligible Alberta SR&ED in Year T, the first $1,500,000 (up to baseline) earns 8% ($120,000), while the $1,500,000 of incremental growth above the baseline earns 20% ($300,000), generating a total refundable IEG of $420,000. Only a first-time R&D claimant with a $0 prior two-year baseline that spends the full $4,000,000 in Year T can achieve the theoretical maximum annual grant of $800,000 (20% × $4,000,000).

The IEG phases out linearly for corporations (and associated groups) whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (taken directly from Line 690 of federal Schedule 33) is between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, using the formula [($40,000,000 − (Line 126 − $10,000,000)) / $40,000,000], and is completely eliminated at $50,000,000. To claim the IEG, the corporation must file AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta) within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (which aligns with the 6-month corporate filing due date plus 15 months = 21 months, though in practice it is strictly constrained by the 18-month federal Form T661 deadline because Alberta TRA withholds IEG disbursement until the CRA verifies the federal T661 claim). Claimants and auditors must also observe a critical Form AT29 line-mapping update: for taxation years ending before December 16, 2024, claimants enter the federal amount from Line 559 of Form T661, whereas for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, claimants must use the federal current SR&ED expenditure amount from Line 557 of Form T661.
British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Atlantic Provinces

Across the remaining Canadian jurisdictions, provincial R&D tax incentives follow distinct statutory rules integrated into the federal T2 return. In British Columbia, claimed on T2 Schedule 425 (Form T666), the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit provides a 10% refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs up to the applicable expenditure limit, and a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years) for other corporations or expenditures exceeding the limit. Having previously operated under periodic five-year sunset extensions (such as the extension to September 1, 2027), BC Budget 2026 eliminated the sunset date and made the BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent. In Manitoba, governed by Section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) and claimed on T2 Schedule 380 (T2SCH380) within 1 year after the corporate filing due date (18 months after year-end), the province provides a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017. For in-house R&D in Manitoba, one-half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years), whereas R&D carried out under contract with an eligible educational institution or research institute is 100% refundable (full 15% refundable). As noted above, if a corporation wishes to renounce the non-refundable portion so it does not grind the federal SR&ED pool, the renunciation must be filed within 6 months of the taxation year-end for federal purposes.

In Saskatchewan, the province provides a 10% refundable R&D tax credit exclusively for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of qualifying expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable credit on excess expenditures and for non-CCPCs (subject to an overall combined annual cap of $1,000,000 in credit) on Schedule 403. In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador each provide a flat 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all eligible corporations (regardless of CCPC status or corporate size) with no annual expenditure cap, claimed via Schedules 340, 360, and 301 respectively. Finally, the Yukon territory provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit (plus an additional 5% bonus, totalling 20%, on payments made to Yukon University) on Schedule 442.

body.text: Administrative Compliance, Updated Form T661 Architecture, and the Pre-Claim Approval Process
The Statutory 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Record Retention Rules

Compliance with the statutory filing deadline under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act is an absolute, non-discretionary jurisdictional bar. A corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred (equivalent to 12 months after the standard 6-month corporate T2 filing due date; for example, a taxation year ending December 31, 2024 has an absolute statutory deadline of June 30, 2026). Neither the Minister of National Revenue nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses discretionary authority under the taxpayer relief provisions (subsection 220(3.2)) to grant an extension of time for an SR&ED claim filed even one day past the 18-month deadline. If a claimant fails to submit the prescribed forms—specifically Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals)—containing both the specific technical project descriptions and the exact expenditure amounts on each prescribed line on or before the 18-month mark, the expenditures are permanently barred from being classified as SR&ED. Moreover, once the 18-month window closes, a claimant cannot amend its Form T661 to add new projects or reclassify upward any expenditure line item that was omitted before the deadline. Pursuant to subsection 230(4) of the Act, all technical, experimental, and financial records supporting an SR&ED claim must be retained by the taxpayer for a minimum period of six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
Granular Line-by-Line Audit Guide to the Updated Form T661 (2025/2026 Version)

To implement the legislative reforms of Bill C-15 and the administrative modernization announced in Budget 2025, the CRA issued a substantially revised version of Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) alongside updated Guide T4088. In Part 1 (General Information), the form captures corporate identification, business number, taxation year dates, and contact information. In Part 2 (Project Technical Data, where a separate Part 2 must be filed for each claimed project), Line 207 requires claimants to select the five-digit Field of Research (FOR) code (RDF#####) from the Statistics Canada Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 (listed beginning on page 18 of Guide T4088) that most accurately classifies the primary scientific or technological field in which the project sought to achieve an advancement, which may differ from the corporation's commercial NAICS industry code. On Lines 212 and 214 (Pre-Claim Approval Identification), if the project received upfront validation through the CRA's new pre-claim approval process, the claimant must tick the box on Line 212 and enter the official CRA pre-claim approval case number on Line 214. Across Lines 242, 244, and 246 (Core Technical Narrative), the claimant must articulate, first on Line 242, what scientific or technological uncertainties the claimant attempted to overcome (maximum 350 words); second on Line 244, what work was performed in the taxation year to overcome those uncertainties, structured chronologically around hypotheses formulated, experiments or analyses conducted, and results observed (maximum 700 words); and third on Line 246, what scientific or technological advancements were achieved or attempted as a result of the work (maximum 350 words). Finally, in Part 2 on Lines 262 and 263 (Project-Level Capital Expenditure Tracking), the claimant must list on Line 262 the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 that were used in that specific project and claimed on Line 390, and report on Line 263 the percentage of total operating time for each property listed on Line 262 (calculated by dividing the property's operating time in that project by its total operating time across the entire taxation year, or across the post-December 15, 2024 period if the taxation year began before December 16, 2024).

In Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures for the Section 37 Pool), the claimant makes its irrevocable election between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method on Line 160. Line 350 reports lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada (excluding GPOEF if using the Proxy Method). Line 355 captures lease costs of equipment used primarily (50% to less than 90% of operating time) for SR&ED; under the Proxy Method, the claimant enters 50% of eligible lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (excluding GPOEF), whereas under the Traditional Method, the claimant must enter "0". Line 390 records total capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 meeting the ≥ 90% ASA test.

In Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes) and Part 5 (Prescribed Proxy Amount), Part 5 computes the 55% PPA on the eligible directly engaged salary base (applying the Specified Employee cap of min(75% × Total Salary, 2.5 × YMPE)). Part 4 integrates current expenditures, the PPA, the 80% conversion of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, Line 535 (capital expenditures for new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024), and Shared-Use Equipment inclusions, and deducts provincial and federal government assistance on Lines 429 and 513 to yield Line 557 (current SR&ED expenditures) and Line 559 (total qualified SR&ED expenditures transferred to Schedule 31).

In Part 6 (Project Costs Breakdown across Parts 6A, 6B, and 6C), Part 6A allocates salaries, materials, contracts, and leased equipment costs across each project number (Line 750), where the total of the leased equipment column in Part 6A must equal the exact sum of Line 350 plus Line 355 from Part 3. Part 6B reports the 20 most expensive depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 across all projects claimed in the taxation year: Box 780 captures the property name (matching Line 262), Box 782 records the full capital expenditure acquisition cost (including purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, and transportation), and Box 786 lists the comma-separated project numbers matching Line 750. Part 6C reports the 20 most expensive Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) properties acquired after December 15, 2024 across all projects: Box 788 captures the SUE property name, Box 790 records the purchase date in YYYY-MM-DD format, Box 792 records 25% of the full capital cost of the SUE property, Box 794 captures the term indicator (entering 1 for first-term SUE or 2 for second-term SUE), and Box 796 lists the comma-separated project numbers matching Line 750.

In Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information and Statutory Penalty Regime), the form mandates complete disclosure of whether any external claim preparer (consultant, accounting firm, or legal advisor) participated in preparing the claim, including the preparer's name, Business Number, billing arrangement code (distinguishing contingency fee percentages from flat or hourly billing), and the total fees paid, payable, or expected to be paid. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if any required information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a mandatory $1,000 penalty is assessed, for which the claimant corporation and the external claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.
Special Protocol for Classified National Security Projects

Where a federal government agency has formally designated one or more of a claimant's R&D project descriptions as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant must not transmit the classified technical narratives through standard tax centre processing. Instead, the claimant must prepare and retain on file internally a fully completed Form T661 containing all Part 2 project descriptions, file the T2 return and Form T661 omitting the classified narratives, and dispatch a formal explanatory letter to the Technical Guidance Division, SR&ED Directorate, Canada Building, 344 Slater Street, 16th Floor, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5, confirming that the specified project descriptions constitute classified national security information and are available for secure inspection upon request.
The New Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and CRA Audit Workflow

To address long-standing industry criticism regarding the retrospective unpredictability of SR&ED reviews, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. This program allows businesses to obtain a formal, upfront technical determination from the CRA confirming that their planned R&D work satisfies the subsection 248(1) eligibility criteria before incurring significant project expenditures, or shortly after project commencement. To qualify for the Pre-Claim Approval Process, the applicant must satisfy both Business Criteria and Project Criteria: under the Business Eligibility Criteria, the applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, must have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and must be in good standing with the CRA regarding tax compliance; under the Project Eligibility Criteria, the project must not have been included in any previous SR&ED claim and must not involve technical or legal issues currently under litigation before the courts.

The application follows a streamlined three-step digital workflow through the CRA's My Business Account portal. In Step 1 (Request a Case Number), the business confirms its eligibility criteria online and obtains an official Pre-Claim Approval Case Number. In Step 2 (Complete the Application), the business responds to structured technical questions detailing the project's scientific or technological uncertainty, planned hypotheses, and experimental methodology, attaching supporting planning documentation. Businesses may also book a free, personalized one-on-one guidance session with a CRA representative prior to submission by emailing OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca or attending the CRA's MS Teams pre-claim approval webinars. In Step 3 (Submit via My Business Account and 8-Week Determination), upon upload through My Business Account, the CRA evaluates the planned project and issues a formal determination within eight weeks. Once approved, the claimant enters the case number on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 when filing its year-end tax return.

When an SR&ED claim is filed with the T2 return, it undergoes automated risk scoring by the CRA's national intake system. The CRA's published service standards—and its verified 2025–2026 operational performance—establish a benchmark of 60 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim for claims accepted as filed (in 2025–2026, the CRA met this standard 95.0% of the time, surpassing its 90% target) and 180 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim for refundable claims selected for technical or financial review (in 2025–2026, the CRA met this standard 92.5% of the time, while no statutory service standard applies to non-refundable claims selected for review). If a claim is selected for full examination, the CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a domain specialist holding engineering or scientific credentials—to audit Part 2 project eligibility against subsection 248(1), alongside a Financial Reviewer (FR) to audit Part 3, Part 4, Part 5, and Part 6 expenditure substantiation, including payroll ledgers, time-tracking sheets, T4 summaries, subcontractor contracts, and capital asset invoices. If the RTA or FR proposes adjustments, they issue a draft SR&ED Review Report; the claimant is afforded 30 days to submit additional contemporaneous evidence before a Notice of Reassessment is issued, after which formal dispute resolution proceeds via an Administrative Second Review or a Notice of Objection to the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the Notice of Reassessment.
Strategic Audit Conclusions and Tax Governance Recommendations

The statutory convergence of Federal Budget 2025 (enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026), the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures, the creation of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category, and the launch of Québec's consolidated CRIC regime has elevated the complexity—and potential non-dilutive yield—of Canadian R&D tax planning to unprecedented levels. To maximize statutory entitlements while insulating claims against adverse reassessment before the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada, corporate tax directors, legal counsel, and technical leads should institutionalize five core governance protocols.

First, corporate tax teams must execute dual-method phase-out modelling and evaluate subsection 127(10.31) elections annually. Every CCPC whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 must model its Expenditure Limit under both the default taxable capital formula and the newly enacted three-year average gross revenue election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32). For capital-intensive private corporations in biotechnology, clean energy, semiconductor hardware, and deep technology whose balance-sheet equity or debt exceeds $15,000,000 while three-year average gross revenue remains lower, filing the prescribed revenue election preserves up to $2,100,000 in annual 35% refundable credits.

Second, enterprises must institutionalize point-of-acquisition intent documentation for restored capital assets. Because eligibility for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures on Line 390 and Part 6B (Boxes 780–786)—as well as Shared-Use Equipment in Part 6C (Boxes 788–796)—hinges legally on the taxpayer's intent at the time of acquisition to utilize the asset ≥ 90% (or > 50% for SUE) of its operating time in Canadian SR&ED, corporations must embed an SR&ED capital authorization memorandum into their procurement workflow. Retroactive assertions of capital intent during an audit are routinely rejected by Financial Reviewers, and equipment usage logs must be maintained continuously to substantiate Line 263 operating-time percentages and prevent recapture.

Third, closely held corporations must structure Specified Employee compensation exclusively as base salary. Because bonuses and profit-linked remuneration paid to Specified Employees (≥ 10% shareholders or non-arm's-length family members) are statutorily disqualified, and dividends do not constitute salaries or wages, CCPCs must pay technical founders regular payroll salary up to the optimal YMPE thresholds ($186,500 for maximum PPA proxy generation in 2026, or up to $373,000 for maximum direct SR&ED salary inclusion) within 180 days of fiscal year-end, accompanied by timely filing of Form T1174 across associated entities.

Fourth, R&D teams must embed quantitative metrics and failure logs into real-time engineering workflows. As demonstrated by the divergent outcomes in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King versus Biscuiterie Dominic inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 97), DAZZM, and Vortex Energy, the Tax Court of Canada strictly enforces the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. Engineering and food or materials science teams must replace qualitative observations with dated, quantitative experimental metrics—such as latency benchmarks, memory throughput, pH, water activity, microbial counts, and tensile failure logs—captured contemporaneously in Git commit histories, Jira tickets, and laboratory notebooks linked directly to specific hypotheses.

Fifth, eligible claimants should leverage the April 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process and optimize multi-provincial stacking. Corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 embarking on multi-year R&D initiatives should submit a Pre-Claim Approval application via My Business Account prior to incurring major expenditures to lock in technical eligibility within eight weeks, reporting the resulting case number on Form T661 Lines 212 and 214. Concurrently, multi-provincial claimants must coordinate their provincial filings—accounting for the $3,000,000 OITC cap and non-refundable ORDTC assistance grind in Ontario, the post-March 25, 2025 CRIC pre-commercialization expansion and modified exclusion threshold in Québec, and the two-year rolling baseline of the IEG on Form AT29 in Alberta—well in advance of the strict 18-month statutory reporting bar.
